contrastMetadata.transferBoundary: Choose hashing when the decisive signal is equality-based membership or frequency state; choose sorting when the result or later reasoning requires ordered adjacency, ranges, or deterministic traversal.

items.prompt: A stream must report whether each arriving identifier has been seen before; result order follows arrival order and no sorted output is required. Which primary signal is strongest?

options.text: Equality-based membership state favors a hash set.
Sorting is required because duplicate detection always needs adjacency.
Compare only consecutive arrivals.
Binary-search the unsorted arrivals.

feedback.reason: The decisive operation is repeated equality-based membership lookup.

blocks.text: Maintain a set containing exactly the identifiers from earlier arrivals. For each new identifier x, first test whether x is in the set, emit that Boolean for the current stream position, and then insert x. Checking before insertion distinguishes a prior occurrence from the current item, and processing in arrival order preserves the required output order. With a conventional hash set this uses expected O(1) time per arrival and O(k) memory for k distinct identifiers. Sorting can detect duplicates only after accumulating and reordering data, so it misses the immediate per-arrival contract. A hard memory cap or deterministic worst-case requirement would reopen the comparison.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_all: Sorting can expose adjacent duplicates after the full input is available, but it cannot emit the required seen-before result at each arrival.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.compare_neighbors: A repeated identifier may be separated from its earlier occurrence by many other values, so comparing only consecutive arrivals loses valid matches.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_search_unsorted: Binary search needs a sorted search domain or another monotonic predicate; the accumulated arrivals provide neither.

items.prompt: A report must emit one group per distinct value in ascending value order, with all equal input values contributing to the same group. Which signal favors sorting?

options.text: The output requires deterministic value order and equal-run adjacency.
Hash lookup is expected O(1), so ordering requirements can be ignored.
The implementation should contain one loop.
Only first-seen membership matters.

feedback.reason: Sorting directly creates the adjacency and order consumed by the result.

blocks.text: Sorting turns equal values into contiguous runs and orders those runs by value. After O(n log n) comparison sorting, one linear scan starts a group when the value changes and accumulates every equal item into that group; emitting runs from left to right already satisfies ascending output. A hash map can also accumulate by equality, but ordinary hash iteration does not guarantee ascending keys, so its complete strategy needs a later sort of the k distinct keys and must include that O(k log k) phase. The reusable rule is to favor ordering when both adjacency and deterministic order are consumed directly by the result.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_expected: Expected O(1) key updates can build counts, but a plain hash table still needs an ordering phase before it can emit ascending groups.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_pass_name: The number of loops says nothing about whether equal values become adjacent or group keys become ascending.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_seen_only: First-seen membership preserves arrival order, whereas this contract explicitly requires value order and complete equal-value groups.

items.prompt: Keys support equality and a compatible hash function but have no meaningful total order. The task asks only whether a queried key exists. Which strategy signal is valid?

options.text: Hash lookup matches the equality contract without inventing an order.
Sorting is mandatory for every lookup problem.
Equal-run grouping is the primary requirement.
Sort by memory address to create a semantic order.

feedback.reason: Hashing requires equality and a compatible hash function, whereas sorting requires an ordering relation.

blocks.text: Membership asks whether some stored key is equal to the query; it does not ask which key is smaller. A hash set stores keys in buckets chosen by their hash and confirms a match with equality, so a compatible hash function—equal keys always hash compatibly—is enough. Comparison sorting is not merely unnecessary here: without a domain-defined total order, it has no legal comparator on which to base sorted search. Memory or worst-case guarantees may affect the final implementation, but the semantic signal is equality-keyed state. Memory-address order is incidental runtime state and cannot replace the missing domain contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorting_required: Sorting requires a comparator that defines a consistent total order, and the prompt deliberately provides no such relation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.group_runs: Grouping equal runs is useful after ordering, but the output asks only one equality-membership decision and consumes no groups.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.index_order: Memory addresses are incidental, may change between executions, and do not define semantic order between the keys.

items.prompt: Records are comparable by timestamp, and the query asks for every record in a time interval in chronological order. Which signal is primary?

options.text: Ordered range traversal favors sorting or an ordered representation.
Hash equality lookup is sufficient.
Only frequency counting is relevant.
The task is duplicate detection.

feedback.reason: Range queries depend on relative order, not only equality.

blocks.text: The query consumes two order operations: locate the first timestamp inside the lower boundary, then traverse records in increasing timestamp until the upper boundary is passed. Sorting once by timestamp makes both operations legal; a lower-bound search finds the start in O(log n), and emitting k matching records takes O(k). A hash table can retrieve an exact timestamp key but does not expose all keys between two timestamps or their chronological order. If data changes frequently, an ordered dynamic structure may replace a static sorted array, but the primary signal remains relative order rather than equality.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_equality: Exact equality lookup cannot locate the first key above a lower bound or traverse every key inside an ordered interval.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.frequency_only: Counting records discards their timestamps and does not emit the requested interval in chronological order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_duplicate: The contract asks for all records in a time range; it states no duplicate-detection objective.

items.prompt: A one-pass job must count occurrences of each hashable token, the caller accepts groups in arbitrary order, expected hash bounds are acceptable, and O(k) memory fits for k distinct tokens. Which primary signal favors hashing?

options.text: Direct key-to-count updates favor a hash map.
Sort because every frequency table must be ordered.
Count only adjacent equal tokens.
Reorder the original token sequence.

feedback.reason: The required state is an equality-keyed count per token.

blocks.text: The required state is one counter per equality class. Scan the tokens once; for token x, look up x in the map, create count 1 if absent, or increment the existing count. Under the stated hash model, n updates take expected O(n) time and the map stores O(k) entries for k distinct tokens. Because output order is arbitrary, iterating those entries needs no later key sort. Sorting could also make equal tokens adjacent, but it adds ordering work and may require copying or mutation that this result never consumes. Deterministic guarantees or insufficient memory would reopen the choice.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_for_order: The caller explicitly accepts arbitrary group order, so imposing value order is not required by correctness.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.adjacent_only: Occurrences of one token may be separated across the entire stream; comparing only adjacent inputs undercounts them.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mutate_input: Reordering the original sequence neither creates the required counters nor follows from the output contract.

items.prompt: Given at least two orderable numeric values, a task asks for the pair with minimum absolute difference, not their original positions. Which signal favors sorting over a hash table?

options.text: After sorting, the minimum difference must occur between adjacent values.
Exact membership is the only required relation.
Expected constant-time hash operations prove optimality.
The task is only to detect duplicates.

feedback.reason: Sorting creates a structural adjacency invariant for the distance objective.

blocks.text: Sort the values as b[0] ≤ … ≤ b[n−1], then compare each adjacent difference b[i+1] − b[i]. For any nonadjacent pair b[i], b[j] with i < j, the interval between them is a sum of adjacent nonnegative gaps, so at least one adjacent gap is no larger than b[j] − b[i]. Therefore some closest pair is adjacent after sorting. Sorting costs O(n log n) and the scan O(n); duplicates correctly produce difference zero. A hash table exposes equality, including the zero-distance case, but cannot locate predecessor or successor values needed when the minimum difference is nonzero.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.membership_only: Exact membership answers whether a specified value exists; it does not identify the nearest values by magnitude.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_constant: Expected constant-time bucket operations do not expose predecessor or successor relationships, so they do not prove a closest-pair algorithm.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicate_only: Duplicates settle only the zero-distance case; when all values are distinct, the algorithm must still compare ordered gaps.

items.prompt: Input is already sorted, and the task is to output value-frequency groups in that same order. Which strategy is most direct?

options.text: Scan consecutive equal runs without building a hash table.
Build a hash map because hashing is always faster than sorting.
Sort the already sorted input again.
Perform random membership queries for every value.

feedback.reason: The existing order already supplies duplicate adjacency and deterministic group order.

blocks.text: The input already contains the structure the output consumes: equal values are adjacent and different runs appear in value order. Start a count at the first value, increment it while the next value is equal, emit the value and count when the value changes, then start the next run. Every element is visited once, so the scan takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary state beyond the output. Re-sorting repeats completed work, while hashing spends O(k) entries for k groups and then still needs ordered emission. The transfer rule is to consume a proven existing order directly before paying to rebuild another index.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.rehash_all: The ordering work is already done and a run scan is linear with constant auxiliary state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.resort: Sorting an already sorted input preserves the same order while adding redundant comparison work.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.random_lookup: Membership queries do not accumulate complete run counts or emit them in the existing sorted order.

items.prompt: A task must return the original index of the first occurrence of each distinct value while preserving first-seen order. Which signal favors a hash-based design?

options.text: Store first indices in a hash map while scanning the original sequence.
Sort values alone and infer original indices afterward.
Only sorted adjacency matters.
Binary-search the unsorted original sequence.

feedback.reason: The required relation is equality lookup coupled with original-position metadata.

blocks.text: Scan the original sequence from left to right. For value x at index i, test whether x is already in a hash map; if not, store firstIndex[x] = i and append (x, i) to the output, otherwise leave the earlier record unchanged. The first insertion proves i is the earliest index, and appending at that moment makes output order equal to first-seen order without relying on hash iteration. This takes expected O(n) time and O(k) state for k distinct values. Sorting values alone destroys both provenance and arrival order; sorting indexed records could preserve identity but would still need a later original-order restoration.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_values_only: Sorting values without attached indices loses which original occurrence supplied each value, especially when duplicates exist.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.adjacent_groups: Sorted adjacency groups by value order, whereas the contract requires earliest indices emitted in first-seen order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_search: The original sequence is not declared sorted, so binary search has no legal half-discard rule.

items.prompt: Objects have a canonical total-order key with deterministic tie-breaking but are expensive to hash. The result needs one deterministic ordered traversal and no later equality queries. Which signal favors sorting?

options.text: The result consumes total order directly, while hashing would add unused lookup state.
The presence of keys implies a hash map.
Expected linear build cost dominates every other contract.
Any one-pass implementation is automatically preferable.

feedback.reason: The strategy should serve the relation the result consumes.

blocks.text: The result consumes the canonical comparator directly: comparison sorting establishes the exact deterministic order, then one linear traversal emits it. Hashing would compute an expensive representation, allocate lookup state, and still fail to provide the required order without sorting its keys or entries afterward. Because no later equality query reuses that state, the hash build has no compensating benefit. The complete sort lifecycle is O(n log n) comparisons plus O(n) output traversal; the real constant cost depends on the comparator, but the contract already requires its order. If repeated equality queries were added, a hash or hybrid representation would become a candidate.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_word: Having keys does not imply equality lookup; here their canonical total order is the relation consumed by the output.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.expected_linear: The hash function is expensive, the state is never reused for queries, and hash iteration still does not satisfy deterministic order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_pass: A one-pass traversal cannot emit arbitrary unsorted input in canonical order unless some prior mechanism has established that order.

items.prompt: A problem statement contains the word "lookup," but the actual query asks for the smallest key not less than x. What should drive the choice?

options.text: The successor-order relation, which favors sorting or an ordered structure.
The word "lookup," which proves hashing.
Any hash table because expected lookup is constant.
Variable names such as key and table.

feedback.reason: The semantic query is an ordered boundary search, not equality membership.

blocks.text: The requested result is the lower bound of x: the first key k in sorted order for which k ≥ x. A static sorted array can find that boundary by binary search, and a dynamic ordered tree can maintain the same successor relation across updates. A plain hash table can test whether x itself exists, but its buckets expose no information about the smallest larger key when x is absent. The word lookup describes an action in ordinary language; it does not define equality semantics. The transfer rule is to translate the output into its exact relation—equality, predecessor, successor, rank, or range—before choosing a representation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.keyword_lookup: The word lookup does not distinguish exact equality from successor, predecessor, rank, or range search.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_any: Expected constant-time equality lookup cannot identify the smallest stored key greater than an absent query value.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.scan_names: Variable names describe implementation vocabulary and provide no correctness or ordering invariant.

items.prompt: A problem requires both exact membership queries and final ascending output. What is the correct initial conclusion?

options.text: Both lookup and ordering signals exist; compare the full workload or use a hybrid design.
Hashing automatically satisfies ascending output.
Sorting makes every exact query expected O(1).
Choose only from query cost and ignore final output.

feedback.reason: Mixed contracts can justify sorting, hashing plus key sorting, or maintaining both representations.

blocks.text: Neither signal can be ignored. One sorted representation costs O(n log n) to build, answers exact membership in O(log n), and already supports a final O(n) ascending traversal. A hash set costs expected O(n) to build and expected O(1) per membership query, but ordinary hash iteration is unordered, so final ascending output adds a sort of the k distinct keys in O(k log k). Maintaining both may improve a large query workload at the price of two representations and synchronized updates. The choice therefore depends on q, k, mutation, memory, required guarantee type, and whether one representation can serve both phases.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_always: Ordinary hash iteration has no ascending-order guarantee, so hashing alone leaves the final output contract unsatisfied.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_always: Sorting is a legal candidate, but its O(log n) membership queries may lose to a reusable hash set when q is large and memory fits.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_output: Final ascending output is observable behaviour and must be included in both correctness and lifecycle cost.

items.prompt: Which result contracts primarily require equality-keyed state? Select all that apply.

options.text: Repeated equality-based membership tests.
Incremental counts by key with arbitrary output order.
Retaining first-seen indices while scanning original order.
Finding the next greater key and emitting an ordered range.

feedback.reason: Hashing is strongest when the state is keyed by equality and does not require ordered traversal.

blocks.text: Equality-keyed state associates information with the exact key rather than with its relative position:

items: Membership stores whether an equal key has appeared.
Frequency stores and increments a counter for each equal key.
First index stores metadata on the first insertion; a separate append at that moment preserves first-seen output order.

blocks.text: The successor/range option instead asks which keys are next or lie between ordered boundaries. Equality alone cannot answer that relation, so it points toward a sorted or ordered representation. The transfer rule is to ask what information is keyed by equality and whether output consumes any order beyond first-seen scan order.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.range_successor: Finding a successor and traversing a range require relative order between different keys, not equality-keyed state alone.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.membership: A set directly records whether an equal key exists and supports repeated membership tests.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.frequency: A map updates the counter associated with the token's equality class on every occurrence.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.first_index: A map records metadata only on first insertion, while the original scan determines first-seen order.

items.prompt: Which result contracts primarily consume relative order or adjacency? Select all that apply.

options.text: Deterministic ascending output.
Grouping equal values into consecutive runs.
Reporting values in an ordered interval.
Only arbitrary-order exact membership on unorderable keys.

feedback.reason: Sorting is valuable when relative order becomes reusable structure.

blocks.text: Relative order is useful when the result consumes a sequence relation:

items: Ascending output directly reads the sorted sequence from smallest to largest.
Equal-value grouping uses the fact that sorting makes every equality class one contiguous run.
An ordered interval uses lower and upper boundaries plus traversal between them.

blocks.text: Exact membership on unorderable keys asks only whether an equal key exists and consumes none of those relations, so equality-keyed state is the primary signal there. The reusable distinction is whether different keys must be compared with each other or only matched for equality.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.arbitrary_membership: Arbitrary-order exact membership consumes equality for one key and does not require relative order between different keys.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.ordered_output: Sorting directly establishes the ascending sequence that the output must expose.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.adjacent_groups: Sorting makes every equality class contiguous, allowing one run scan to form groups.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.range_query: Range reporting needs ordered boundary location and traversal between those boundaries.

items.prompt: Which questions should be answered before choosing hashing or sorting? Select all that apply.

options.text: Does the result require equality lookup, relative order, or both?
Are keys hashable, comparable, or both?
Must original order, deterministic group order, or indices be preserved?
What are the query and update volumes, memory and mutation limits, and required expected or worst-case guarantees?
Is a variable named map or sorted?

feedback.reason: The decision follows semantic operations and observable contracts.

blocks.text: A final choice needs four independent checks:

items: Relation: equality membership or per-key state favors hashing; successor, range, adjacency, or deterministic value order favors ordering.
Legal key operations: hashing needs compatible equality and hash; sorting needs a consistent comparator.
Observable preservation: original indices, arrival order, mutation permission, grouping order, and duplicate semantics constrain legal transformations.
Lifecycle and resources: build, queries, updates, output, memory, mutation, and guarantee type determine which legal candidate is feasible and cheaper.

blocks.text: A variable name is not evidence for any of these obligations. The transfer rule is to establish semantic legality first, then compare the complete workload rather than a single advertised operation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.variable_name: Names such as map or sorted are implementation vocabulary and establish neither a required relation nor a legal cost model.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.relation: Without the exact relation, a strategy may optimize equality while the result consumes order, or the reverse.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.key_contract: A strategy is illegal when keys lack its required compatible hash/equality contract or total comparator.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.observable_order: Order, indices, duplicate identity, and mutation are correctness constraints rather than optional implementation details.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.workload_resources: Query count, updates, memory, mutation, and guarantee type determine feasibility and total lifecycle cost.

items.prompt: Which situations can make both hashing and sorting correct candidates? Select all that apply.

options.text: Determine whether any duplicate exists in a reorderable array.
Count values and then emit keys in ascending order.
Serve many membership queries and later produce ordered output.
Keys support neither hashing nor a comparison contract.

feedback.reason: Correctness can leave multiple strategies available.

blocks.text: Each selected situation admits two complete, correct paths:

items: Duplicate existence: insert into a set and stop on a repeated key, or sort a reorderable array and scan adjacent values.
Ordered frequencies: sort and count equal runs, or count in a hash map and then sort the k distinct keys for output.
Many memberships plus final order: sort once and binary-search queries, or use expected-fast hashing for queries and sort keys at the final phase; a hybrid may retain both.

blocks.text: Keys that support neither a compatible hash/equality contract nor a comparator make neither standard candidate legal. When both are legal, the final choice follows from query volume, memory, mutation, guarantees, key-operation cost, and which preprocessing later phases can reuse.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unhashable_unorderable: Without compatible hashing/equality or a comparison contract, neither a standard hash table nor comparison sorting is directly legal.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.duplicate_exists: A set detects a repeated key by equality, while sorting exposes repeated keys as adjacent values.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.frequency_ordered: Sort-and-run and hash-then-sort-distinct-keys both satisfy counts plus ascending output.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.many_membership_final_order: A sorted index, a hash-then-sort lifecycle, or a synchronized hybrid can all satisfy both phases.

items.prompt: Which observations fail by themselves to establish even a substantive equality-keyed signal for hashing? Select all that apply.

options.text: The prompt uses the word "lookup."
A hash operation is expected O(1).
The input contains duplicates.
The task requires only equality membership and keys are hashable.

feedback.reason: Surface vocabulary and isolated operation costs do not determine the strategy.

blocks.text: A semantic signal must connect the output to equality-keyed state:

items: The word lookup may describe a successor, range, or rank query rather than equality.
Expected O(1) describes one hash operation, not whether that operation computes the required relation.
Duplicates can be handled by equality-keyed counts or by sorting them into adjacent runs.

blocks.text: By contrast, a contract requiring only exact membership on hashable keys does establish a real hash mechanism signal, though memory and guarantee constraints still decide whether that legal candidate is selected. The transfer rule is to separate semantic relevance from final cost ranking.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.equality_only: Exact membership on hashable keys directly consumes equality-keyed state, so it is a substantive hash signal even though later resource checks still apply.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.word_lookup: The word lookup does not reveal whether the query is equality, successor, predecessor, rank, or range.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.expected_o1: An isolated operation bound does not show that equality lookup is the relation required by the result.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.duplicates: Duplicate presence alone supports both hashing by equality and sorting into adjacent equal runs.

items.prompt: Arrange the decision process for distinguishing a lookup signal from an ordering signal.

elements.text: State the exact observable result and query relation.
Check whether legal equality/hash and total-order operations exist.
Identify whether membership state or ordered adjacency/ranges will be reused.
Compare memory, mutation, guarantees, and workload before selecting the strategy.

feedback.reason: The strategy follows from the relation and reusable structure required by the contract.

blocks.text: Use the decision dependencies in this order:

items: State the observable result and translate the query into equality, per-key state, successor, range, adjacency, or ordered traversal.
Check whether keys legally support compatible hashing/equality, a total comparator, or both.
Identify which created structure will be reused: membership state, key-associated metadata, sorted adjacency, or ordered boundaries.
Compare complete build, query, update, output, memory, mutation, and guarantee costs for the remaining legal candidates.

blocks.text: Each step constrains the next: costs are meaningful only for legal mechanisms, and legal mechanisms are relevant only when they support the exact result relation. The transfer boundary is a changed query, preservation contract, workload, or resource limit.

items.prompt: An array of n hashable keys receives q exact membership queries. Compare building a hash set once with sorting once and using binary search, assuming expected O(1) hash operations and in-place comparison sorting.
constraints: Hash-set build uses O(n) auxiliary entries.
In-place comparison sort uses O(log n) stack space.
Input mutation is allowed for the sorting candidate.
Membership answers are emitted one at a time; output storage is excluded from auxiliary space.

sort_time: O(n log n + q log n)
O(n log n + q log n)

sort_time.sort_and_binary_queries: O(n log n + q log n)

feedback.reason: The lookup signal favors expected hash time, while sorting offers an ordered representation and lower stated auxiliary memory under these assumptions.

blocks.text: Derive each lifecycle from its stated operation model:

items: Hashing performs n expected O(1) insertions and q expected O(1) membership tests, so expected time is O(n + q). The table retains up to n keys, giving O(n) auxiliary space.

Sorting performs O(n log n) comparisons once. Each of q binary searches takes O(log n), so total time is O(n log n + q log n). The stated in-place algorithm reuses the input and needs O(log n) stack space.

blocks.text: These bounds do not make hashing universally preferable: the hash bound is expected, the sort mutates input, and ordered output or expensive hashing can change the end-to-end decision. The transfer rule is to compare setup plus q times query cost and to keep auxiliary space separate from input and streamed output.

contrastSets.transferBoundary: Choose hashing when the decisive signal is equality-based membership or frequency state; choose sorting when the result or later reasoning requires ordered adjacency, ranges, or deterministic traversal.
